questions.q: The editorial quotes a saying of the Prophet on how good qualities are gained. What does it say of knowledge and of serenity?
options: Knowledge comes through learning, and serenity through exercising patience
Yes. One who strives for good receives it.
Knowledge comes with age, and serenity with sleep
Not quite. The article says: Knowledge comes through learning, and serenity through exercising patience.
Knowledge comes by birth, and serenity by wealth
Not quite. The article says: Knowledge comes through learning, and serenity through exercising patience.
Knowledge comes by luck, and serenity by solitude
Not quite. The article says: Knowledge comes through learning, and serenity through exercising patience.
questions.rationale: “A person gains knowledge through learning, even-mindedness; and serenity comes from exercising patience; one who strives to find good, receives good.”

questions.q: Everything man needs to live is already provided on earth and nowhere else we know of. What does the article say is expected of him in return?
options: To leave the earth as he found it
Not quite. The article says: To acknowledge God of his own free choice, without seeing Him and without compulsion.
To use as much as he can
Not quite. The article says: To acknowledge God of his own free choice, without seeing Him and without compulsion.
To explore the other planets
Not quite. The article says: To acknowledge God of his own free choice, without seeing Him and without compulsion.
To acknowledge God of his own free choice, without seeing Him and without compulsion
Right. The rest of creation acknowledges Him by compulsion.
questions.rationale: “Exceptionally, God has created man as a free creature. Man is required to acknowledge God by his own choice.”

questions.q: What “silent message” does the article say a tree gives to man?
options: Shed what you have every year
Not quite. The article says: Learn the art of conversion – turn whatever you receive, even the unpleasant, into something good.
Grow tall and overshadow others
Not quite. The article says: Learn the art of conversion – turn whatever you receive, even the unpleasant, into something good.
Stand firm and never move
Not quite. The article says: Learn the art of conversion – turn whatever you receive, even the unpleasant, into something good.
Learn the art of conversion – turn whatever you receive, even the unpleasant, into something good
Well read. As the tree turns soil, water and light into growth.
questions.rationale: “Every tree gives a silent message to man: Learn the art of conversion and the whole world will become a means of spiritual food for you.”

questions.q: “If you throw a stone at a tree, it will give you fruit in return.” What does the article call this?
options: A reason to guard orchards
Not quite. The article says: The highest kind of positive behaviour.
The highest kind of positive behaviour
Yes. Answering harm with benefit.
An accident of nature
Not quite. The article says: The highest kind of positive behaviour.
A sign of weakness
Not quite. The article says: The highest kind of positive behaviour.
questions.rationale: “If you throw a stone at a tree, it will give you fruit in return. This is the highest kind of positive behaviour.”

questions.q: Asked whether the last night of Ramadan was the “night of power,” what did the Prophet reply about the forgiveness granted on it?
options: “No one can know”
Not quite. The article says: “No, but as soon as the deed is done, the reward for the deed is immediately bestowed”.
“No, but as soon as the deed is done, the reward for the deed is immediately bestowed”
Correct. Hence it is called the “night of reward.”
“Yes, it is the same night”
Not quite. The article says: “No, but as soon as the deed is done, the reward for the deed is immediately bestowed”.
“It depends on the moon”
Not quite. The article says: “No, but as soon as the deed is done, the reward for the deed is immediately bestowed”.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet replied, ‘No, but as soon as the deed is done, the reward for the deed is immediately bestowed’.”

questions.article: Living in a World of Professions
questions.q: What imbalance does the article find in people of our “world of professions”?
options: They change professions too often
Not quite. The article says: They are highly developed in their professions but underdeveloped in the science of life.
They are highly developed in their professions but underdeveloped in the science of life
Right. Able at work, at a loss in living.
They earn more than they need
Not quite. The article says: They are highly developed in their professions but underdeveloped in the science of life.
They know too little about their own trades
Not quite. The article says: They are highly developed in their professions but underdeveloped in the science of life.
questions.rationale: “While everyone is a developed personality in terms of their profession, in terms of their own nature, everyone is an underdeveloped personality.”

questions.article: Living in a World of Professions
questions.q: What “simple formula” does the article recommend?
options: Make intellectual development your priority, and manage the other parts of life around it
Well reasoned. A question of priority, not just balance.
Earn first and think later
Not quite. The article says: Make intellectual development your priority, and manage the other parts of life around it.
Give equal hours to work and rest
Not quite. The article says: Make intellectual development your priority, and manage the other parts of life around it.
Leave your profession altogether
Not quite. The article says: Make intellectual development your priority, and manage the other parts of life around it.
questions.rationale: “Adopt a simple formula: make intellectual development your priority and then try to manage all other aspects of your life.”

questions.q: The reviewer says we have two eyes for the visible world and a “third eye.” What is it, and what is it for?
options: Imagination – by which we invent stories
Not quite. The article says: The intellect – by which we can understand the unseen world.
The intellect – by which we can understand the unseen world
Yes. Reflection reaches where sight cannot.
Instinct – by which we sense danger
Not quite. The article says: The intellect – by which we can understand the unseen world.
Memory – by which we recall the past
Not quite. The article says: The intellect – by which we can understand the unseen world.
questions.rationale: “The third one is called ‘intellect’. It is the most important for us as we can understand the unseen world with the help of intellect.”

questions.q: The cells of the body are wholly replaced over the years, yet the person remains the same. What does the review say this indicates?
options: That memory is stored in the bones
Not quite. The article says: That there is something in us beyond the body that does not perish – the soul.
That there is something in us beyond the body that does not perish – the soul
Exactly. So death need not be the end.
That the body never really changes
Not quite. The article says: That there is something in us beyond the body that does not perish – the soul.
That people are different every decade
Not quite. The article says: That there is something in us beyond the body that does not perish – the soul.
questions.rationale: “Our body cells are completely renewed and the old ones get destroyed. We nonetheless remain the same, this indicates that another portion is there which is immortal and that is soul.”

questions.q: Upset by a remark belittling women’s intelligence, the writer heard the Maulana’s answer to a similar question. What had he said?
options: “Women should not concern themselves with it”
Not quite. The article says: “There would be no Islam if not for Hagar”.
“There would be no Islam if not for Hagar”
Well read. Men and women differ in role but are equal in respect.
“Intelligence does not matter”
Not quite. The article says: “There would be no Islam if not for Hagar”.
“Such remarks should be ignored”
Not quite. The article says: “There would be no Islam if not for Hagar”.
questions.rationale: “Maulana replied, Hajira nahi hoti to Islam hi nahi hota (There would be no Islam if not for Hagar).”
